caption:
Lulu feels great after treatment, then stiff again a few days later. So why the exercise homework every time?

Muscles, tendons and bones adapt to the load you give them. Current guidelines for back pain, knee and hip arthritis and many tendon problems put exercise and education first, with hands-on care as a helpful add-on. Treatment can ease things for a while; exercise helps you build on it.

Hybi's tip: pick just three exercises and do them at the same time each day. Three you actually do usually help more than ten you skip.

If exercise makes things worse or nothing changes, get reassessed. Book online via the link in bio

caption:
Strong fingers, cranky shoulders? Momo knows the feeling, especially when the hips sag on steep walls.

Climbing training tends to focus on fingers and pulling, while shoulders, trunk and hips work hard on every reach without much dedicated training. Clinical Pilates can help with shoulder control overhead, trunk tension, usable hip range and some pushing to balance all that pulling.

Hybi's 1-minute builder: side plank, 20 seconds × 3, both sides. One or two sessions a week around climbing days is a common starting point.

Shoulder pain when hanging, or no change after two weeks, is worth an assessment. Book online via the link in bio

caption:
The wave is there, but Momo's pop-up is always a beat late.

A good pop-up is a press, a tuck and a stable landing. Clinical Pilates can train each part: reformer planks and knee tucks for the transition, extension work for paddling endurance through the upper back, hip mobility for a lower stance, and balance work for a moving board.

Hybi's 1-minute drill: plank to knee tuck, alternating sides, 8 reps × 2 sets, slow and controlled. Many surfers fit one or two sessions a week around the forecast.

Pain that lingers after paddling is worth an assessment. Book online via the link in bio

Trails ask for single-leg strength, ankles that react to rocks and roots, and thighs that can control long descents. Clinical Pilates trains that braking skill with slow, controlled returns on the reformer, plus balance and footwork.

Hybi's 1-minute drill: slow step-downs from a low step, 3 seconds each, 8 reps per side. Two Pilates sessions a week alongside hill and stair walks, starting several weeks out, is a practical way to prepare.

caption:
Momo can kick past her head, yet her landings wobble. Many dancers have plenty of flexibility but less strength at end range.

caption:

caption:
Two good weeks, then a rough day that made Koko wonder if anything's working? That's how most recoveries look. Progress zigzags.

A big day, a poor night's sleep or a stressful week can stir things up for a few days, and that usually doesn't mean you're back at square one. Track what you can do, not just how sore you are: stairs, sleep, how long you can sit or walk. Compare this month with last month rather than today with yesterday, ease off a little on bad days, then build up again.

caption:
Forearms cooked and neck stiff after a week of rolling? BJJ and other martial arts ask a lot of the grip, neck, upper back and hips.

Remedial massage can help you feel looser and move more comfortably between sessions. It sits well alongside sleep, sensible training load and strength work rather than replacing them. Keep lighter work for the day or two before a comp or grading, and save firmer sessions for lighter training days. Tell your therapist about any late taps or awkward landings.
